clips.title: He has every reason to be cynical — and he wasn't feeling sorry for himself
clips.why: A story that detonates: an undocumented teenager who may be denied his dream, asked what he wants for his birthday, asks for a book on social justice. The build is real and the payoff reframes the viewer's own self-pity — someone with far less was still looking outward. Heavily replayed by viewers. The leading word 'Club' is the tail of the previous sentence; cut to 'one day after class'. L0214–L0216 ('maybe you're asking yourself, can I really do this') sits just before and could serve as a lifted hook.

clips.end_words: and he's going to bring people along with him
clips.text: Club one day after class I was talking to my students about going to college and one of my top students raised his hand and said that he wasn't sure he could go to college because he's undocumented Ed he wasn't sure if they'd take him last year I took him out to breakfast for his birthday and I wanted to get him a gift so I asked him what he wanted and he just started talking about struggles that he saw other students in his class facing and finally said you know I'd really just like a book on social justice I was blown away here is a young guy who has every reason to be cynical he wasn't sure if the country he calls home the only one he's known was going to deny him his dream of going to college but he wasn't feeling sorry for himself he wasn't even thinking of himself he has a greater sense of purpose and he's going to bring people along with him

clips.title: You're sure someone else is going to do it — but they're not. You will.
clips.why: The build — kids in a dorm assuming a big company would connect the world — sets up one of the cleanest identity handovers in the speech: the thing you're waiting for someone else to do is yours. 'But they're not. You will.' is the landing; cut there, because the rest of L0069 ('it's not enough to have that purpose yourself...') opens a different thought that doesn't pay off inside this clip.

clips.title: An impostor — a 22-year-old kid who had no idea how things actually worked
clips.why: Zuckerberg, with nothing to gain from admitting it, describes the exact 2am feeling: everyone left, everyone wanted to sell, 'I felt alone and worse, it was my fault. I wondered if I was just wrong — an impostor, a 22-year-old kid.' The turn — 'now years later I understand, that is how things work' — converts the doubt from proof of inadequacy into proof of being in the game. Ends on 'that can't stop us from getting started' (the word 'started' opens L0099 — cut there). It is list-shaped in the middle, which is why it ranks below the sharper single-idea clips.

near_misses.why_not: The second landing of the student story ('if a high school senior who doesn't know what the future holds can do his part, we owe it to the world') needs the story before it — 'I can't even say his name' dangles for a stranger, and the combined run exceeds a reel-sized minute.
A list of generational projects (climate, curing disease, online voting) — inspiring at a graduation, but the viewer can pick up nothing about themselves from it.
Rowling's twelve rejections and Beyoncé's hundreds of songs are other people's résumés; 'the greatest successes come from the freedom to fail' is the only takeaway and it arrives generic.
An honest argument about luck, loans and safety nets, but it is policy aimed at the system — it leaves the broke viewer holding the problem rather than something to stand on.
The janitor-at-NASA story and the 'create a world where everyone has purpose' thesis are warm and famous, but they read as civic mission for graduates — the viewer nods instead of replaying.
The closing prayer and 'may your life be a blessing' is a gentle outro — comfort placed without any evidence or turn before it.

The material that works on a 2am viewer is not the civic 'purpose for everyone' thesis but three pockets of personal, identity-level material: the innovation run in the middle (ideas don't come out fully formed, the Eureka lie, being misunderstood, feeling like an impostor at 22), the 'they're not — you will' turn after the Facebook founding story, and the undocumented student story near the close. The rest is graduation-ceremony inspiration aimed at a graduating class, not at the person scrolling alone.
